name_en: Compressed Teas (cake, brick, tuo and ball forms)
processing: Loose finished tea (maocha) is weighed, briefly steamed to soften it, then pressed in a cloth bag under a stone or in a hydraulic press into a shape and dried slowly. Shapes include the round cake (bing, classically 357 g, stacked seven to a bamboo-wrapped tong), the brick (zhuan, 250 g to 1 kg), the bowl-shaped tuo (100–250 g), mushroom and melon shapes, mini tuo of a few grams, dragon balls of 7–8 g, and chocolate-bar slabs scored into squares. A paper ticket (nei fei) is pressed into the cake and a leaflet (nei piao) wrapped with it.
harvest_season: The leaf is picked in spring (prized) or autumn, pressed weeks or months later; the production year on the wrapper is what the market trades on.
appearance_dry: A disc, brick or bowl of leaves pressed tightly enough to hold their shape, with whole leaves and tips visible on the surface and a small paper ticket embedded in it.
appearance_liquor: That of the tea inside: pale yellow for young sheng, red-brown for ripe pu-erh and dark tea, gold for white tea cakes.
appearance_wet: Leaves that separate and unfurl once broken from the cake, often still clumped in the first steeps.
taste_profile: Compression itself adds little taste but slows the tea's contact with air, so compressed teas age more slowly and evenly than loose; a tightly machine-pressed cake brews stronger and ages slower than a loosely stone-pressed one.

brewing.notes: Break the tea off with a pick, working along the layers from the edge so the leaves stay whole rather than crumbling. Rinse once with boiling water, then short steeps; tight tuo and bricks need an extra rinse and a slightly longer first steep to open. A dragon ball is one pot's dose and needs no breaking.

vintage_note: Compressed tea is sold by the production year printed on the wrapper and by its standard weight and shape: 357 g cakes, 250 g or 1 kg bricks, 100 g tuo, 7–8 g dragon balls, plus 100 g and 200 g cakes for the modern market. Sheng and shu pu-erh cakes are traded from the current year back decades, white tea cakes by year as a more recent market, dark-tea bricks (Fu brick with its golden flowers, Qian Liang columns, Liu Bao baskets) by batch year. The wrapper, the nei fei ticket, the factory recipe number and the storage history are all part of the price; famous wrappers are faked, so buy recent years from sellers you trust.
description:
Compressed tea is tea pressed into a shape: a disc, a brick, a bowl, a ball. It began as a way to move tea across China and along the caravan routes to Tibet, Mongolia and Russia without it crumbling or going stale, and it survives because pressing turns out to be good for tea that is meant to age. Pu-erh is the famous case, but dark teas from Hunan, Guangxi and Hubei, and now white tea from Fujian, are pressed too.

The method is gentle. Loose finished tea is steamed for a few seconds to soften it, pressed in a cloth bag under a heavy stone or in a hydraulic press, and dried slowly; a paper ticket naming the maker is pressed into the cake. Stone-pressed cakes are looser and age faster; machine-pressed 'iron cakes' are dense and slow. The classic round cake weighs 357 g and is wrapped in paper and stacked in sevens in a bamboo sheath, which is why the old factory cakes are called 'seven-son cakes'.

Compression changes how you brew more than how the tea tastes. You break off what you need with a pick, working along the layers so the leaves come away whole, rinse it with boiling water and brew it gongfu-style; tight tuo and bricks want an extra rinse. Compressed teas keep their inner leaves away from air, so they age slowly and evenly.

Buying a cake means reading a wrapper: production year, factory or maker, recipe number, region, and the storage it has had. Shapes carry hints too, since tuo and bricks were traditionally made from humbler leaf for trade and cakes from better leaf, though that is no longer a rule. Beware famous old wrappers at bargain prices; they are the easiest thing in tea to counterfeit.

If you are new to it, a 100 g or 200 g cake of a recent year and a tea pick are the right starting point, and a dragon ball is the no-tools way to try one pot of a tea before committing to a whole cake.
history:
Before the Ming dynasty, pressed tea was the normal form of tea in China. Under the Tang and Song leaves were usually ground and moulded into blocks, later broken up, toasted and powdered or boiled. Some bricks were bound with flour or even blood or manure so they would hold up as currency. A block travelled better than loose leaf, which mattered on caravan routes such as the Tea Horse Road toward Tibet. Loose tea took over in China from the Ming onward, while pressed tea stayed essential for trade.

The later history is full of specific shapes. The bowl-shaped tuocha is credited to a Yunnan tea factory in 1917. The 357 g cake came to be known as qizi bing, seven-son cake, because seven were packed together. Pressing also went industrial: the Russian merchant P. A. Ponomarev set up the first industrial tile-tea production in China at Hankou in 1876. Soviet factories made tile and brick tea too, with green brick from Georgia going to Kalmyk, Tuvan and Buryat drinkers, and Kumamoto in Japan exported brick tea to China and Russia from the Meiji era until the Second World War.

Today bricks are less common than they were, but pu-erh and other dark teas are still often pressed, and in those teas the shape belongs to the tea's identity and its ageing.
